History:
- Chief complaint: Wheeze and shortness of breath.
- Onset/duration: 2–3 days.
- Course: Persistent over last few days; worse with walking/exertion; currently feels well at rest.
- Associated symptoms: Dry cough; reports feeling feverish but measured temperature 37°C (afebrile). No chest pain, no sputum production, no hemoptysis, no nocturnal awakening.
- Functional impact: Unable to walk to work; sometimes has difficulty completing sentences during episodes; can climb stairs.
- Triggers/context: Atopic history (hay fever, eczema). No smoking. No specific recent trigger identified.
- Prior episodes: History of asthma since childhood; occasional hospital visits in childhood (no ICU). Adult symptoms suggest intermittent use of reliever inhaler.

Past Medical History:
- Conditions: Asthma (childhood “quite bad”); hay fever; eczema.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.
- Medications: Salbutamol inhaler as needed (uses every few weeks and with exercise); dose/route/frequency not documented. No other regular medications.
- Hospitalizations: Occasional hospital checks for asthma in childhood; no ICU.
- Social: Non-smoker. Alcohol ~1 glass of wine every 2–3 days. Lives with partner. Works as an engineer; currently working from home/sick leave due to symptoms.

Physical Examination:
- Setting: Teleconsultation; no in-person exam.
- Vitals: Not recorded. Patient-reported temperature 37°C.
- General/respiratory: Currently comfortable at rest; denies shortness of breath at rest; able to climb stairs; exertional dyspnea present.
- Chest pain: None.
- Cough: Dry; no sputum; no hemoptysis.
- Night symptoms: None reported.
- Other systems: Not recorded.

Impression:
- Likely asthma exacerbation, mild to moderate, possibly triggered by allergens and/or a viral illness.
- DDx (consistent with transcript):
  - Viral upper respiratory infection with bronchospasm: short duration, dry cough, wheeze.
  - COVID-19 infection precipitating bronchospasm: possible but no classic features reported.

Management Plan:
- Medications/devices:
  - Use salbutamol 2–4 puffs every 4 hours initially (as advised during call).
  - Prescribe spacer; pharmacist to demonstrate technique.
  - Prescribe peak flow meter; pharmacist to demonstrate use.
  - Start regular over-the-counter antihistamine for hay fever (per clinician advice).
- Monitoring:
  - Record peak flow values morning and evening for 1 week.
  - Safety-net: Call back immediately if temperature becomes high or wheeze/shortness of breath worsens.
- Follow-up:
  - Arrange asthma review in ~1 week to assess control and peak flow diary; may need additional controller medication depending on response.
- Work/activities:
  - Continue to limit exertion as needed until symptoms improve.

Patient Summary:
- 34-year-old with childhood asthma and atopy presents with 2–3 days of wheeze, exertional dyspnea, and dry cough; afebrile by measurement. Current picture consistent with an asthma flare.
- Plan includes increased reliever use with spacer, peak flow monitoring, antihistamine for atopy, and close follow-up in one week with earlier review if worsening.

Key Takeaways:
- Use salbutamol regularly at 2–4 puffs every 4 hours initially, with a spacer.
- Start daily antihistamine and monitor peak flow twice daily for one week.
- Seek medical advice promptly if fever develops or breathing/wheeze worsens.

Next Steps:
- Pick up spacer and peak flow meter from pharmacy and receive instruction on use.
- Schedule follow-up in one week to review symptoms and peak flow diary; consider adding controller therapy if indicated.
- Call sooner if deterioration occurs.

Quality checks:
- Missing elements: No objective vitals (RR, HR, SpO2), no in-person respiratory exam, no peak flow readings yet, medication dosing not fully documented (salbutamol dose/route/frequency unspecified beyond current plan), no asthma action plan discussed, no documentation of vaccinations or recent infectious exposures/testing.
- Conflicts: Patient initially implied stopping inhalers 3–4 years ago but later stated they “normally” use salbutamol as needed (conflict noted). Reported “fever” but measured 37°C (afebrile; clarified).
- Transcript quality: Generally clear; some answers were hesitant/uncertain with minor ambiguities around inhaler use and timing.
